items.title: When Beauvoir's Le Deuxieme Sexe appeared
items.claim: Simone de Beauvoir's Le Deuxieme Sexe was published in which year?
items.reveal:
The book contains the often-cited line 'On ne nait pas femme: on le devient' ('One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman').

The Vatican placed it on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1956.
items.why: A single publication can crystallise a long intellectual movement and trigger immediate institutional reaction.

items.title: What the Academie recommends instead of 'email'
items.claim: The Academie francaise has recommended a French alternative to 'email'. What is it?
items.reveal:
Quebec coined 'courriel' first; the Academie endorsed it in 2003. Similar recommendations include 'mot-diese' (hashtag) and 'jeu video en nuage' (cloud gaming).

Usage in France varies; 'mail' and 'email' remain common in practice.
items.why: Official terminology and everyday usage often diverge, sometimes lastingly.

items.title: Loi Toubon
items.claim: France's loi Toubon (1994) requires French in certain official contexts. Which is closest to what it covers?

options.text: It bans English speech in private homes
It requires French in commercial advertising, employment contracts and public-sector communication, with alternatives in foreign languages permitted but a French version also required
It applies only to government emails
It applies only to broadcast television

items.reveal_title: It mandates French in public commercial and administrative contexts
items.reveal:
The law was originally proposed by Jacques Toubon (then Minister of Culture). Some clauses were softened by the Constitutional Council on freedom-of-expression grounds.

Enforcement is sporadic but has produced occasional fines.
items.why: Language policy is most visible at the interface between commerce and state.
